dataset: US bar, court and legislative guidance on lawyers' use of generative AI: primary sources
license: CC BY 4.0 for this index; each linked document keeps its issuer's own terms

fields.jurisdiction: two-letter state code, DC, or US for national bodies
fields.issuer: the body that issued the document
fields.title: the document's own title
fields.number: opinion, notice or chapter number as the issuer cites it, or null
fields.date: YYYY-MM-DD when the document states a day, else YYYY-MM, else YYYY when only the year is known (the entry's notes then say how the year was established)
fields.kind: formal_opinion | advisory_opinion | guidance | court_notice | court_policy | rule_amendment | statute
fields.url: primary source only: the issuing bar, court, association or legislature
fields.url_verified: date MV2 last checked the URL
fields.verification: fetched = the page or file was retrieved and its title matched; cited = the URL is the issuer's own address, taken from the issuer's site or from search results for that page, and was not retrieved
fields.confidentiality_note: MV2's one-sentence paraphrase of the confidentiality point, not a quotation
fields.in_house_tools_note: what, if anything, the document says about tools run inside the firm, or null
fields.notes: anything a reader should know, or null

entries.issuer: American Bar Association, Standing Committee on Ethics and Professional Responsibility
entries.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence Tools
entries.confidentiality_note: Before entering client information into a generative AI tool, a lawyer must weigh the risk that it reaches people outside the firm, and also people inside the firm who would not know the information came from a client and protect it.
entries.in_house_tools_note: Says self-learning tools raise a cross-matter disclosure risk even when used only inside one firm, because one client's input can surface in another lawyer's prompt.
entries.notes: The ABA site returned HTTP 403 to MV2's automated fetch on 2026-10-13; the URL is the one the ABA and secondary sources cite. The ABA published further guidance on AI in law firms in January 2026, not indexed here yet.

entries.issuer: Alaska Bar Association, Ethics Committee
entries.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence & The Practice of Law
entries.confidentiality_note: Before using generative AI for a client, a lawyer should understand to a reasonable degree how the tool works, what its limits are, and whether it can keep client confidences and secrets safe.
entries.notes: The 9-page PDF was retrieved and its title matches the Alaska Bar's own chronological index, which links to it and lists no later AI opinion as of 2026-10-14. MV2's tool did not extract the PDF text; the approval date and the paraphrase come from the search index's text of the same file. A WSBA blog summary says the opinion encourages closed systems or anonymised prompts; MV2 has not confirmed that wording in the PDF.

entries.issuer: Alabama State Bar, Office of General Counsel
entries.title: Artificial Intelligence Use: Best Practices Under Existing Professional Conduct Rules
entries.confidentiality_note: Lawyers must protect confidential client information when using AI and understand how a vendor processes and keeps what is entered; the opinion contrasts tools that do not train on inputs with free consumer versions and warns that prompts and interaction logs may be discoverable.
entries.notes: MV2 read the text of the 11-page PDF on 2026-10-14. It states no date and no opinion number on its face, so only the year is recorded: the file sits under /assets/2026/05/, it cites an Alabama decision of 24 April 2026 and a source dated 18 February 2026, and Law360 reported it on 24 July 2026. The number comes from the bar's HTML page for the opinion (alabar.org/office-of-general-counsel/formal-opinions/artificial-intelligence-use-best-practices-under-existing-professional-conduct-rules/), which was fetched and whose title matches. Its Rule 1.6 section recommends closed, non-training enterprise systems over free consumer tools, anonymised or substitute identifiers, documented client consent where risks remain, and firm retention policies that cover AI interaction logs. Also covers agentic AI, fees and supervision.

entries.issuer: Supreme Court of Arizona, Steering Committee on Artificial Intelligence and the Courts (AISC)
entries.title: Generative AI: Ethical Best Practices for Lawyers and Judges
entries.confidentiality_note: Confidential or nonpublic information must not go into a tool unless the user has enough assurance that the tool will not share or use it; free tools may protect little even with a training opt-out, and before entering client information into a tool that risks disclosure the lawyer should get the client's informed consent.
entries.in_house_tools_note: Contrasts open, free tools with enterprise-level tools or tools customised for the firm or court, which may give more assurance that inputs are not revealed or used, and cites Florida 24-1 on in-house tools; when in doubt it still advises leaving confidential information out.
entries.notes: MV2 read the text of the 6-page PDF, dated 14 November 2024 on its first page. Written by a Supreme Court committee for both lawyers and judges, separately from the State Bar's practice guidance (az-best-practices). Also covers billing, court disclosure, bias and supervision, says prospective clients talking to a firm's chatbot should be told so, and suggests a written AI policy that staff acknowledge.

entries.issuer: State Bar of Arizona (Practice 2.0)
entries.title: Guidance for the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in the Practice of Law in Arizona
entries.confidentiality_note: Do not enter confidential client information into an AI tool without adequate safeguards, read its terms to confirm inputs are neither shared nor used for training, anonymise data on public platforms, and keep data and recordings on encrypted, access-controlled platforms, checked with IT or security specialists.
entries.notes: The page shows no date; 2025 is the year of the earliest dated State Bar reference MV2 found, a 9 December 2025 news release that links it, and some trackers place it in late 2024. Practice guidance, not an ethics opinion: Arizona's formal opinions now come from the Supreme Court's Attorney Ethics Advisory Committee, which had issued none on AI as of the bar's 2026 billing FAQ. Also asks for client notice and consent before AI records or summarises client meetings. The older address /practice-tools-management/state-bar-of-arizona-ai-guidance returned 404 on 2026-10-14.

entries.issuer: State Bar of California, Standing Committee on Professional Responsibility and Conduct
entries.title: Practical Guidance for the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in the Practice of Law
entries.confidentiality_note: A lawyer must not put confidential client information into a generative AI tool that poses material confidentiality or security risks without the client's informed consent, and must take reasonable steps, beyond trusting marketing claims, to learn how the tool collects, uses, stores and discloses what is entered, consulting IT or security experts where needed.
entries.in_house_tools_note: Says a tool that neither trains on nor shares inputs may still lack adequate security, that risk rises from isolated prompt tools to integrated systems to autonomous agents, and that agentic systems with access to firm email, document stores or client files need a limited scope, monitoring and access controls so they cannot leak information across matters or send it out without human review.
entries.notes: The 2026 revision, approved by the Board of Trustees on 14 May 2026 (per the bar's Ethics & Technology Resources page), replaces the November 2023 version and adds agentic AI at the California Supreme Court's request. MV2 read the text of the 9-page PDF on 2026-10-14; its executive summary says it replaces the 2023 version. The 2023 file was at calbar.ca.gov/Portals/0/documents/ethics/Generative-AI-Practical-Guidance.pdf. Separately, proposed amendments to Rules 1.1, 1.4, 1.6, 3.3, 5.1 and 5.3 on AI went out for public comment in 2026 (the second comment period closed 6 August 2026); MV2 found no Supreme Court order adopting them as of 2026-10-14. California's statute on lawyers' AI use, effective 1 January 2027, is ca-sb-574. Also covers fees: subscription costs for general AI tools are overhead.

entries.issuer: California Legislature (Senate Bill 574, approved by the Governor)
entries.title: SB 574: Attorneys, arbitrators, judicial officers, and alternative resolution providers
entries.confidentiality_note: From 1 January 2027 an attorney may not enter confidential, personal identifying or other nonpublic information into a generative AI system unless access to it is limited to the attorney and authorised persons who are themselves bound to keep it confidential; the same new section bars delegating the practice of law to generative AI and requires reasonable steps to check AI output, including every citation.
entries.in_house_tools_note: Law-firm summaries say the confidentiality test turns on who can access what is entered, not on whether a product is public, enterprise or run by the firm; none of the summaries MV2 read mentions self-hosted tools.
entries.notes: Adds Business and Professions Code section 6068.1 and amends Code of Civil Procedure section 128.7 so that no court filing may contain a citation the responsible attorney has not personally verified; also bars arbitrators from delegating decisions to generative AI (new CCP section 1282.1) and has the Judicial Council revisit its standard on judges' use of it. Attorneys must also disclose generative AI use to the court for documents they submit; commentators note the law does not say what form that takes. Signed 30 September 2026 (the Governor's office release of that date, which MV2 fetched, lists it), effective 1 January 2027. leginfo.legislature.ca.gov returned HTTP 403 to MV2's automated fetch on 2026-10-14, so the statute text was not read: the chapter number comes from a Morgan Lewis alert (2 October 2026) and the paraphrase from Holland & Knight (1 October 2026), Morgan Lewis and Alston & Bird summaries. The first state statute on lawyers' use of generative AI, according to those firms.

entries.issuer: Supreme Court of Colorado
entries.title: Rule Change 2026(02): Colorado Rules of Professional Conduct, Preamble and Scope and Rule 1.1
entries.confidentiality_note: A new comment to Rule 1.1 lists the rules a lawyer's use of technology, particularly AI, can implicate, among them preserving client confidential information under Rule 1.6, and a new Scope paragraph says a lawyer may be disciplined for violations that result from using technology directly or indirectly.
entries.notes: MV2 read the text of the 6-page PDF (redline and clean versions): amended and adopted by the Court en banc on 8 January 2026, effective immediately. It adds Scope [20A], aligns Comment [8] to Rule 1.1 with the ABA Model Rule's technology-competence wording, and adds Comment [9]. The Colorado Lawyer (May/June 2026) describes it as the first AI-specific amendment to a state's lawyer conduct rules. MV2 found no Colorado Bar Association formal ethics opinion on AI; one vendor site cites a 'Formal Opinion 145' on AI that MV2 could not confirm.

entries.issuer: District of Columbia Bar, Legal Ethics Committee
entries.title: Attorneys' Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Client Matters
entries.confidentiality_note: Do not enter client confidences or secrets into a generative AI tool unless reasonably satisfied the provider will not see, keep or reuse them; otherwise use another product, negotiate zero retention, or enter only non-confidential information.

entries.issuer: The Florida Bar, Board Review Committee on Professional Ethics
entries.title: Florida Bar Ethics Opinion 24-1 (generative AI)
entries.confidentiality_note: A lawyer should get the affected client's informed consent before using a third-party generative AI program that would disclose confidential information.
entries.in_house_tools_note: States that if an in-house generative AI tool is used and no confidential information is disclosed to a third party, informed consent under Rule 4-1.6 is not required.
entries.notes: The page notes that advisory ethics opinions are not binding.

entries.issuer: Supreme Court of Florida
entries.title: In re: Amendments to Florida Rule of General Practice and Judicial Administration 2.515
entries.confidentiality_note: The amendment says nothing about confidentiality: it makes every signer of a Florida court filing, lawyer or self-represented, represent that the legal authorities cited exist and are accurately cited, and lets courts sanction filings that break that representation.
entries.notes: MV2 read the text of the 6-page per curiam opinion of 28 May 2026, adopted on the Court's own motion. It adds subdivision (d)(2)(D) to Rule 2.515, effective 15 June 2026 at 12:01 a.m.; sanctions, after notice and an opportunity to be heard, may include reprimand, contempt, striking the document, dismissal, costs and attorneys' fees. The court commentary says the amendment is mainly a statewide, uniform replacement for varied circuit court administrative orders on disclosing and certifying AI use in filings. The Florida Bar News report of 29 May 2026 (floridabar.org/the-florida-bar-news/supreme-court-amends-rules-to-address-ai-use-in-court-filings/), also fetched, says a follow-up administrative order bars courts from imposing their own AI disclosure or certification requirements; MV2 has not read that order. Comments were due by 11 August 2026; MV2 has not checked for a later opinion on them. The Bar's ethics opinion on AI is fl-24-1.

entries.issuer: State Bar of Georgia (Law Practice Management Program and Special Committee on Artificial Intelligence and Emerging Technology)
entries.title: Generative AI Toolkit
entries.confidentiality_note: Do not put confidential client information into a generative AI tool that lacks adequate confidentiality, anonymise client data, check a vendor's security, and consider informed consent; standard click-through terms may exclude any duty of confidentiality, which enterprise plans with contractual data limits address.
entries.notes: A living document; the first version is dated July 2025 and the current one is reported as last updated 9 July 2026, which matches the internal modification stamp of the 16-page PDF MV2 retrieved. MV2's tool did not extract the PDF text; the paraphrase comes from the Rule 1.6 and 5.3 sections of the bar's own AI and Emerging Technology page (gabar.org/programs/law-practice-management/ai-and-emerging-tech), which links the toolkit. Secondary sources say the bar chose a toolkit instead of a formal advisory opinion.

entries.issuer: Supreme Court of Hawaiʻi (letter of Chief Justice Mark E. Recktenwald to the Hawaii State Bar Association)
entries.title: Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the Practice of Law in Hawaiʻi
entries.confidentiality_note: Gives initial guidance that the existing Hawaiʻi rules already govern lawyers' use of AI, names Rule 1.6 on confidentiality among the rules every lawyer using AI should know, and points to ABA Opinion 512's duty to protect client information.
entries.notes: The letter, dated 21 January 2025 and addressed to the HSBA president for circulation to members, is Appendix 4 of the Committee on Artificial Intelligence and the Courts' final report to the Hawaiʻi Supreme Court (dated 15 December 2025, filed 16 December 2025 in SCMF-24-0000305); MV2 read the report's pages. The letter also lists Rules 1.1, 1.3, 1.4, 1.15, 3.1, 3.3, 3.4 and 5.3 and Hawaiʻi Rules of Civil Procedure 11 and 37. The report says a proposed order and declaration on AI use in court filings was under consideration by the Supreme Court, and its Appendix 3 holds the Judiciary's own AI guardrails for staff. MV2 found no Hawaii State Bar formal ethics opinion on AI.

entries.issuer: Illinois Attorney Registration and Disciplinary Commission (ARDC)
entries.title: The Illinois Attorney's Guide to Implementing AI
entries.confidentiality_note: Explains how generative AI works and why that matters for confidentiality and security, and gives a framework for choosing and documenting tools, with sample office policies, client notices, a consent form and a terms-of-use checklist.
entries.notes: Nonbinding; the ARDC page says the Supreme Court's AI policy governs if the two conflict (see il-supreme-court-ai-policy). The page links the guide as an online flipbook and gives no date; October 2025 is the month of the ISBA's announcement. Written with solo and small-firm lawyers in mind.

entries.issuer: Supreme Court of Illinois
entries.title: Illinois Supreme Court Policy on Artificial Intelligence
entries.confidentiality_note: AI use by lawyers, litigants and court staff is authorised if it meets legal and ethical standards, and AI applications must not compromise sensitive information such as confidential communications, personal identifying information or protected health information.
entries.notes: Announced 18 December 2024, effective 1 January 2025. An administrative policy of the Court, not a rule change: it says existing rules suffice and that disclosure of AI use should not be required in a pleading. The two-page policy PDF, linked from the announcement, is hosted on the courts' file store at ilcourtsaudio.blob.core.windows.net and was retrieved.

entries.issuer: Indiana Supreme Court
entries.title: Indiana Rules of Trial Procedure, Rule 11: Parties represented by an attorney: Signing, certification, and verification (as amended by order 2026-26S-MS-8)
entries.confidentiality_note: The amended rule says nothing about confidentiality: an attorney's signature on any filing, including one prepared with the help of artificial intelligence, now also certifies that every cited legal authority is authentic, and a court may strike a filing that does not comply.
entries.notes: MV2 read the current text of Rule 11 and of new Rules 11.1 and 11.2 on the Indiana Supreme Court's official rules site (rules.incourts.gov) on 30 October 2026. The Rule 11 page shows the version amended on 14 July 2026 by order 2026-26S-MS-8 and in effect from 1 August 2026: 11(B) adds the certification that cited legal authority is authentic, and 11(F) says the rule covers filings prepared with the assistance of artificial intelligence, the internet or other resources. New Rule 11.1, effective the same day, applies the same certification to self-represented parties; new Rule 11.2 lists citing fictitious legal authority among conduct that can support a finding that a filer is an abusive litigant, after which a court may set conditions on further filings and, after a chance for a hearing, impose sanctions up to dismissal with prejudice and attorneys' fees. The order itself (in.gov/courts/files/order-rules-2026-26S-MS-8.pdf), which also amends Trial Rules 8, 9.2, 30 and 87, had not yet been read by MV2. One tracker reported an expected effective date of 1 October 2026; the official rules site shows 1 August 2026. None of the three rule pages requires disclosing the use of AI.

entries.issuer: Kentucky Bar Association
entries.title: The Ethical Use of Artificial Intelligence ("AI") in the Practice of Law
entries.confidentiality_note: Lawyers keep their duties of competence and confidentiality when using AI, and need not disclose routine AI use to a client unless the work is outsourced, the client is charged for it, or disclosure is otherwise required.
entries.notes: The KBA also publishes a sample AI use policy (April 2026) that refers to this opinion.

entries.issuer: Supreme Court of Louisiana (letter from its General Counsel, at the Justices' request, to the Louisiana State Bar Association)
entries.title: The Emergence of Artificial Intelligence
entries.confidentiality_note: The Court says the existing rules already cover AI in its current forms and that Louisiana lawyers remain responsible for protecting confidential client information, citing Rule 1.6 among the rules that apply unchanged.
entries.notes: MV2 read the text of the 2-page letter, dated 22 January 2024, addressed to the LSBA president for circulation to members and signed by the Court's General Counsel; the LSBA hosts it and links it from its news page. Besides Rule 1.6 it lists Rules of Professional Conduct 1.1, 1.3, 1.4, 1.15, 3.1, 3.3 and 5.3 and Code of Civil Procedure articles 371 and 863, and it says the Court's Technology Commission and Rules Committee will keep the Justices informed of any need for rule changes. No rule was changed.

entries.issuer: Massachusetts Office of Bar Counsel (article by an Assistant Bar Counsel)
entries.title: Two Years of Fake Cases and the Courts are Ratcheting up the Sanctions
entries.confidentiality_note: The article is about fabricated citations and mentions confidentiality only in a footnote, which names the possible disclosure of confidential information as another important risk of AI and points to Rules 1.6, 1.9(c) and 1.18(b).
entries.notes: MV2 read the text of the 7-page PDF on the Board of Bar Overseers' public file store. It shows no date; it cites a decision of 30 July 2025 and an online case list last accessed in August 2025, so it was written in or after August 2025, and only the year is recorded. It reviews court sanctions for fabricated citations, including two Massachusetts Superior Court decisions (February 2024 and June 2025), and recommends firm AI policies covering the risks, citation checking, communication within work teams, incident response and ongoing training. The article says it is for general information and has no substantive legal effect; it is not an ethics opinion. The Office's articles index (massbbo.org/s/articles-on-ethics) could not be read as text by MV2's tool.

entries.issuer: State Bar of Michigan (Ethics)
entries.title: Artificial Intelligence for Attorneys: Frequently Asked Questions
entries.confidentiality_note: Enter only information that is not privileged or protected where possible; if protected client information must go into an AI program, get the client's consent first under MRPC 1.6(c)(1) and take reasonable steps to confirm the provider safeguards it.
entries.notes: The page says last updated November 2024, with a fees answer added 11 February 2025 (building a firm-wide AI tool, in-house or through a vendor, is overhead, not billable to one client). For judges, see the State Bar's judicial ethics opinion JI-155 (October 2023), not indexed here because it is addressed to judicial officers.

entries.issuer: Director, Minnesota Office of Lawyers Professional Responsibility (column in Bench & Bar of Minnesota)
entries.title: Ethics guidance for generative AI use
entries.confidentiality_note: Many generative AI tools keep inputs to learn from, which risks unauthorised disclosure, so using most tools beyond simple idea generation will generally need the client's informed consent, and boilerplate in an engagement letter is not enough.
entries.in_house_tools_note: Points out that ABA Opinion 512 explains how client information can be improperly disclosed even with in-house-only generative tools.
entries.notes: A column by the director of the regulator, Susan M. Humiston, in the State Bar's journal (September 2024), applying ABA 512 to Minnesota; not a formal Lawyers Professional Responsibility Board opinion. The reprint on lprb.mncourts.gov returned 404 on 2026-10-14. The MSBA's AI Working Group report (June 2024, adopted August 2024) is about unauthorised practice and access to justice and is not indexed separately.

entries.issuer: Office of Legal Ethics Counsel & Advisory Committee of the Supreme Court of Missouri
entries.title: Informal Opinion 2024-11 (generative AI and a firm AI policy)
entries.confidentiality_note: A firm planning to use a generative AI service must vet its terms of use, how securely it holds what is entered, how the provider uses that data and what sources it draws on, as part of the reasonable efforts Rule 4-1.6(c) requires.
entries.notes: Written for a lawyer drafting a firm AI policy. Treats outside AI vendors under the Rule 4-5.3 guidance for nonlawyer service providers and cross-refers to Missouri's earlier cloud-computing opinion 2018-09.

entries.issuer: Office of Legal Ethics Counsel & Advisory Committee of the Supreme Court of Missouri
entries.title: Informal Opinion 2026-09 (AI software in depositions)
entries.confidentiality_note: Before putting confidential information into AI software used in depositions, including tools that listen in real time, the lawyer must get the client's informed consent after discussing the tool with them.
entries.in_house_tools_note: Names the risk inside the firm that an AI tool draws on one client's information when working for another client, alongside the risk of exposure to outsiders.
entries.notes: Says the ethics rules do not themselves require disclosing AI use to the court, opposing counsel or the deponent, but other rules, orders and privacy laws may.

entries.issuer: North Carolina State Bar
entries.title: Use of Artificial Intelligence in a Law Practice
entries.confidentiality_note: Lawyers should avoid putting client-specific information into publicly available AI tools, and must make reasonable efforts under Rule 1.6(c) to safeguard client information.
entries.in_house_tools_note: Says the lawyer remains responsible for keeping information secure whether the AI tool is hosted by a vendor or run on the firm's own servers.

entries.issuer: North Dakota Court System
entries.title: Public Notice on the Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI)
entries.confidentiality_note: Anyone using AI must take care that confidential communications, personal identifying information, protected health information, juvenile, sealed or restricted records and anything else protected by law or court rule are not disclosed, and the duty to safeguard that information stays with the person using the tool.
entries.notes: MV2 read the text of the 2-page notice dated 1 June 2026. It says AI use is not prohibited and that the courts do not require disclosure of AI use in filings solely because AI was used, though other rules or orders may; filers stay fully accountable under N.D.R.Civ.P. 11, must confirm every citation independently and may not rely on AI for legal judgments; courts keep their authority under N.D.R.Ct. 11.5 to strike filings and impose sanctions. It applies to attorneys and self-represented litigants and may be updated. A notice, not a rule change.

entries.issuer: New Hampshire Bar Association, Ethics Committee
entries.title: Ethics of Using Artificial Intelligence in Practice
entries.confidentiality_note: Under Rule 1.6(c) a lawyer must understand how an AI tool uses and stores what is entered and whether anything keeps it from third parties, starting with the tool's terms and privacy policy, which may allow the provider to use submitted information.
entries.notes: An Ethics Corner article, which the Committee describes as general guidance on the New Hampshire Rules of Professional Conduct, not a formal opinion. It was submitted to the Board of Governors at its 8 February 2024 meeting and is dated 15 May 2024 in the bar's article list. Also covers supervision under Rules 5.1 and 5.3 and firm AI policies; it does not discuss client consent.

entries.issuer: Supreme Court of New Jersey (Notice to the Bar)
entries.title: Legal Practice: Preliminary Guidelines on the Use of Artificial Intelligence by New Jersey Lawyers
entries.confidentiality_note: Existing Rules of Professional Conduct, including confidentiality, apply unchanged to AI use; the guidelines cover accuracy, candor, confidentiality, preventing misconduct and oversight.
entries.notes: A 30 March 2026 Notice to the Bar adds a sample starter AI policy template and encourages firms to adopt written AI policies.

entries.issuer: New Jersey State Bar Association, Task Force on Artificial Intelligence (AI) and the Law
entries.title: Task Force on Artificial Intelligence (AI) and the Law: Report, Requests, Recommendations, and Findings
entries.confidentiality_note: Before adopting an AI tool a firm should find out and document how client data is transmitted, used and stored and judge from that whether the tool can keep it confidential, and every firm should adopt a written AI policy with a risk assessment framework.
entries.notes: A 36-page report of the bar association's 27-member task force, dated May 2024 on its cover; MV2 read its cover, summary of findings and vendor appendix. Appendices give a sample AI use policy and questions to ask vendors, including data ownership and access, breach notification, retention and deletion, subcontractors and data handling after the contract ends. It also suggests that some responsibility for protecting data may shift to technology providers. A second copy sits under /wp-content/uploads/2025/12/ on the same site. Not an ethics opinion; the Supreme Court's own guidelines are nj-preliminary-guidelines.

entries.issuer: State Bar of New Mexico, Ethics Advisory Committee
entries.title: Using Generative Artificial Intelligence in the Practice of Law
entries.confidentiality_note: Lawyers may use generative AI but must take particular care with confidentiality whenever they enter client information, especially into third-party tools that learn from what users type.
entries.notes: The 9-page PDF was retrieved; its title and date match the search index's text of the same file, which MV2's tool could not extract itself. The number 2024-004 is how trackers cite it; MV2 has not read it from the PDF.

entries.issuer: New York City Bar Association, Committee on Professional Ethics
entries.title: Ethical Obligations of Lawyers and Law Firms Relating to the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in the Practice of Law
entries.confidentiality_note: Lawyers must make sure a generative AI tool meets confidentiality requirements and that anything shared with it is secure, following the format of California's 2023 guidance.
entries.notes: A city bar opinion, not a state-wide one. For the state bar's April 2024 report see ny-nysba-task-force-2024; for the City Bar's later opinions on AI that records calls see ny-nycbar-2025-6 (clients) and ny-nycbar-2026-2 (non-clients).

entries.issuer: New York City Bar Association, Professional Ethics Committee
entries.title: Ethical Issues Affecting Use of AI to Record, Transcribe, and Summarize Conversations with Clients
entries.confidentiality_note: Clients must be told, and must agree, whenever an AI system records their calls; lawyers must safeguard the recordings, transcripts and summaries under Rule 1.6, find out where they are stored, for how long, whether they train the tool and whether they could be reached in discovery, and keep to any no-retention policy they announce.
entries.in_house_tools_note: Distinguishes tools the lawyer controls from tools controlled by a vendor or by the client; it does not address on-premises or locally run tools specifically.
entries.notes: A city bar opinion. Reaffirms the City Bar's Opinion 2003-02 that wanting an accurate record does not justify undisclosed taping, points to two-party consent and biometric-privacy laws, and says lawyers should know how to switch off default recording in meeting platforms and review AI summaries promptly.

entries.issuer: New York City Bar Association, Committee on Professional Ethics
entries.title: Ethical Issues Affecting Use of AI to Record, Transcribe, and Summarize Conversations with Persons Who Are Not Clients
entries.confidentiality_note: Lawyers must get every participant's consent before an AI tool records a call and must understand how the tool stores and shares recordings, transcripts and summaries because confidentiality and privilege are at stake; by default they should not record calls with non-clients at all.
entries.in_house_tools_note: Notes that when a client or another participant runs their own recording tool the lawyer has no control over its security and may not see its transcripts; it does not discuss locally run tools.
entries.notes: MV2 read the text of the 4-page PDF linked from the report page (nycbar.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/20221672-AiRecordingEthicsOpinion.pdf); the page is dated 5 August 2026. Extends Opinion 2025-6 (ny-nycbar-2025-6) to co-counsel, prospective clients, opposing counsel, witnesses and investigators. Warns that witness recordings may be discoverable and that a recording of a prospective client the firm turned down, kept inside the firm, can create Rule 1.18 conflicts. A footnote allows a different balance for a lawyer with a hearing impairment.

entries.issuer: New York State Bar Association, Task Force on Artificial Intelligence
entries.title: Report and Recommendations of the New York State Bar Association Task Force on Artificial Intelligence
entries.confidentiality_note: Treats confidentiality, with competence and supervision, as a core duty when lawyers use AI, and offers a sample engagement-letter clause for telling clients how AI will be used on their matter.
entries.notes: An 86-page report approved by the NYSBA House of Delegates (6 April 2024 per secondary sources), not a formal ethics opinion. The PDF was retrieved; its title matches the search index's text of the same file. NYSBA's later AI work sits with its Committee on Artificial Intelligence and Emerging Technologies.

entries.issuer: New York State Unified Court System (22 NYCRR Part 161; notice posted by the New York State Bar Association)
entries.title: Effective June 1, 2026, The New York State Unified Court System Has Adopted a New Rule Regarding the Use of Artificial Intelligence
entries.confidentiality_note: The notice says nothing about confidentiality: Part 161 lets attorneys use AI tools to prepare court papers without mandatory disclosure, but requires them to review each paper and independently make sure it contains no fabricated or fictitious cases, statutes or other material.
entries.notes: The rule text on nycourts.gov (/rules/chiefadmin/161.shtml) returned HTTP 403 to MV2's automated fetch on 2026-10-30, so the rule itself was not read. The URL is the New York State Bar Association's posting, dated 2 June 2026 and credited to the New York Unified Court System, which MV2 fetched; the effective date, the permission to use AI without mandatory disclosure and the review duty come from it. It says the rule rests on 22 NYCRR 130-1.1 and Rule 3.3 and that individual judges may still adopt their own AI rules. The date recorded is the effective date; MV2 did not find the adoption date.

entries.issuer: Ohio Board of Professional Conduct (staff guidance, at the request of the Supreme Court of Ohio)
entries.title: Ohio Ethics Guide: Artificial Intelligence for Lawyers and Judicial Officers
entries.confidentiality_note: When client-related information goes into AI at all, use only tools with adequate security and confidentiality safeguards, and anonymise client information and avoid identifying details whatever the tool; commentators note these two statements pull in different directions.
entries.notes: Nonbinding staff guidance for lawyers and judges. The 16-page PDF is the copy the Supreme Court of Ohio's AI Resource Library and Court News Ohio link; it was retrieved, but MV2's tool did not extract its text, so the paraphrase rests on passages quoted by the Ohio Employer Law Blog (4 June 2026) and law-firm summaries. Court News Ohio (30 June 2026) says the guide went to Ohio lawyers earlier that month; some firms date it April or 2 June 2026.

entries.issuer: Oregon State Bar, Legal Ethics Committee and Board of Governors
entries.title: Artificial Intelligence Tools
entries.confidentiality_note: Lawyers must understand how an AI tool stores information and whether it collects prompts to train the product for other users, and must check the product and vendor before client information goes in.
entries.notes: The 8-page PDF was retrieved; its heading matches the search index's text of the same file, which MV2's tool could not extract itself. A WSBA summary says it distinguishes closed and open AI models and says when client consent is needed; MV2 has not confirmed that wording in the PDF. Oregon's later opinion on chatbots and AI agents is or-2026-208.

entries.issuer: Oregon State Bar, Legal Ethics Committee and Board of Governors
entries.title: Chatbots and AI Agent Communications
entries.confidentiality_note: Before using a chatbot a lawyer must confirm that what is sent through or stored by it is reasonably secure, which may mean constant encryption, keeping client data out of training, isolating each client's data and vetting the vendor and the products it builds on; what prospective clients type is protected under Rule 1.18.
entries.notes: MV2 read the text of the 8-page PDF, which ends 'Approved by the Board of Governors, February 2026'. Its answer to whether Oregon lawyers may use chatbots with clients and prospective clients is a qualified yes: use clear disclaimers, have a responsible lawyer notified so conversations can be reviewed promptly, run conflict checks on prospective clients, and require lawyer approval for actions an AI agent might take on its own, such as sending an engagement letter.

entries.issuer: Pennsylvania Bar Association and Philadelphia Bar Association (joint)
entries.title: Ethical Issues Regarding the Use of Artificial Intelligence
entries.confidentiality_note: Lawyers must safeguard client information and make sure AI systems that handle confidential data follow strict confidentiality measures; citations produced with AI must be verified.
entries.notes: Secondary sources date it to May or June 2024; MV2 recorded the month most sources give.

entries.issuer: Supreme Court of Rhode Island
entries.title: Interim Guidelines for the Ethical Use of Generative AI by Rhode Island Lawyers
entries.confidentiality_note: Before using any generative AI tool a lawyer should read its terms and privacy policy to learn whether it keeps inputs, whether its confidentiality promises can be enforced, whether breaches are notified and whether inputs survive the end of the service, so that client information is not reachable by people outside the firm or by people inside it who should not have access; a lawyer must tell the client when entering that client's information into a tool.
entries.in_house_tools_note: Says a firm's ethical screens must cover the AI tools it uses so that a screened lawyer cannot reach the matter's information through them, and that a lawyer stays responsible for AI-made advertising whether the tool is run in-house or by a third party.
entries.notes: MV2 read the text of the 7-page PDF on the Judiciary's attorney-resources pages; it begins the same as pages 3-9 of the adopting order (ri-rule-1-1-2026), which gives the date. The order calls the guidelines advisory and subject to revision; lawyers with specific questions are pointed to the Supreme Court's Ethics Advisory Panel. They also say lawyers need not tell clients of every AI use but should consider disclosing regular use in the engagement agreement and must disclose it when a client asks; hourly bills cover only time actually spent and general AI tool costs are overhead; website chatbots carry Rule 1.18 duties to prospective clients; all output and citations must be verified before filing; and even one fabricated citation by opposing counsel may need reporting under Rule 8.3.

entries.issuer: Supreme Court of Rhode Island
entries.title: In re Amendments to Article V, Rule 1.1 of the Supreme Court Rules (Professional Conduct) and Adoption of Interim Generative AI Guidelines
entries.confidentiality_note: The order itself does not address confidentiality: it rewrites Comment [6] to Rule 1.1 so that competence includes keeping abreast of the benefits and risks of existing and developing technology, and adopts interim AI guidelines whose confidentiality section is summarised in ri-interim-guidelines-lawyers.
entries.notes: MV2 read the text of the 14-page order. Section 1 amends Comment [6] to Rule 1.1; Section 2 adopts interim guidelines for lawyers (ri-interim-guidelines-lawyers) and for judicial officers, which the order says neither amend the Rules of Professional Conduct or the Code of Judicial Conduct nor carry the force of law. The entry line reads 'this ___ day of June, 2026' and the extracted text of the signed copy shows 17th filled in, which is the date recorded. The judicial officers' guidelines (pages 10-14) are not indexed separately because they are addressed to judges.

entries.issuer: Supreme Court of South Carolina (order of the Chief Justice)
entries.title: Interim Policy on the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence
entries.confidentiality_note: Court staff may not use AI to process confidential court records or privileged information unless expressly authorised, and lawyers are reminded that their use of generative AI must not compromise client confidentiality or breach the South Carolina Rules of Professional Conduct.
entries.notes: MV2 read the text of the 4-page order, signed by Chief Justice John W. Kittredge on 25 March 2025. It binds judicial branch officers and employees (approved tools on approved devices only, human oversight of anything drafted with AI); for lawyers and litigants it is a reminder, not new regulation, which is why binding is recorded as advisory. It stays in effect until further order. MV2 found no South Carolina Bar formal ethics opinion on AI.

entries.issuer: Professional Ethics Committee for the State Bar of Texas
entries.title: Opinion 705 (generative artificial intelligence)
entries.confidentiality_note: Before entering client information, especially into self-learning programs that store inputs, a lawyer should be reasonably satisfied the program will not reveal confidential information to others, or else consult the client and get consent.
entries.notes: Issued at the request of the State Bar's Taskforce for Responsible AI in the Law.

entries.issuer: Virginia State Bar, Standing Committee on Legal Ethics (approved by the Supreme Court of Virginia)
entries.title: Reasonable Fees and Generative Artificial Intelligence
entries.confidentiality_note: A fees opinion rather than a confidentiality one: hourly bills may reflect only time actually spent, while reasonable flat or value-based fees may reflect the efficiency and skill of using AI, as long as the basis is explained to the client under Rule 1.5(b).
entries.notes: The 4-page PDF was retrieved; MV2's tool did not extract its text, and the search index's text of the same file reads 'Approved by the Supreme Court of Virginia November 24, 2025'. The title here is descriptive; the bar's draft was circulated as 'LEO 1901 Reasonable Fees - Generative AI'. Secondary sources say it departs from ABA 512 and NC 2024 FEO 1 by not requiring flat fees to fall just because AI saved time.

entries.issuer: Virginia State Bar
entries.title: Guidance on Generative Artificial Intelligence
entries.confidentiality_note: Lawyers must understand a tool's terms of service and how it may use what they enter, since many free public tools may show inputs to others or train on them; the page also warns that AI-enabled browsers can be steered by hidden text on malicious sites.
entries.in_house_tools_note: Contrasts free public tools with legal-specific or internally developed products that no one outside the firm can reach, which may protect confidential information, but says the lawyer must still make reasonable efforts to assess their security.
entries.notes: The guidance is a section of the bar's Ethics page and shows no date; August 2024 is the month secondary sources give. The same section points to LEO 1901 on fees and AI, indexed separately as va-leo-1901.

entries.issuer: Washington State Bar Association, Committee on Professional Ethics
entries.title: Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Tools in Law Practice
entries.confidentiality_note: Do not put client information into an AI tool until satisfied it will be protected as RPC 1.6 requires: consumer products often lack confidentiality commitments, and for business tools the lawyer must read and periodically recheck the contract terms, such as use of data for training.
entries.notes: The WSBA gives only the year 2025; one tracker dates it 20 November 2025. Depending on sensitivity, the opinion says a lawyer may need to consult the client or get informed consent, and clients may restrict tools. A PDF copy is on wsba.org at /docs/default-source/legal-community/committees/committee-on-professional-ethics/ao-202505.pdf.

entries.issuer: State Bar of Wisconsin (Ethical Dilemma column by its ethics counsel, Wisconsin Lawyer)
entries.title: Ethical Considerations When Using Generative Artificial Intelligence
entries.confidentiality_note: Before entering confidential client information into a generative AI tool a lawyer must weigh the risk that others reach it, and, following ABA Opinion 512, the column says informed consent is needed before client information goes into self-learning tools and that boilerplate in an engagement letter is not enough.
entries.in_house_tools_note: Warns that even a firm's own proprietary generative AI tool can surface one client's confidential information in answer to another lawyer's prompt and pass it to another client of the firm.
entries.notes: MV2 read the article page, dated 4 October 2024 (Wisconsin Lawyer vol. 97, no. 9, October 2024; cited as 97 Wis. Law. 29-32), and retrieved the 4-page PDF of the same pages. It applies ABA Formal Opinion 512 to the Wisconsin rules (SCR 20) and says it examines only that opinion. A column by the State Bar's ethics counsel, not a formal ethics opinion; MV2 has not checked the State Bar's formal opinions for AI. Also covers client communication (a lawyer must answer honestly if asked about AI use and follow a client's request not to use it), fees, candor and supervision.

entries.issuer: West Virginia Lawyer Disciplinary Board (Office of Disciplinary Counsel)
entries.title: Artificial Intelligence
entries.confidentiality_note: A lawyer should get the client's informed consent, confirmed in writing, before using generative AI on the client's matter, and keeps the duties of confidentiality, supervision and verification.
entries.notes: The URL is the Office of Disciplinary Counsel's opinion index, which lists 'L.E.O. 2024-01 Artificial Intelligence' and links the PDF on a third-party file host (storage.googleapis.com); the older wvodc.org/pdf/AILEO24-01.pdf address now returns 404. The date and the paraphrase come from secondary summaries of the PDF. The index lists no later AI opinion as of 2026-10-14.
